property_summary: For any contract state, paused() returns the actual paused flag (_paused) (i.e., sometimes true and sometimes false depending on prior pause/unpause calls); the mutant always returns true, violating that when the real contract is unpaused after a pause/unpause sequence.

For every admissible input sequence, C.paused() returns the actual paused state (false if not paused, true if paused); the mutant always returns true, so there exist inputs where C.paused() == false but mutant.paused() == true.

For every call, the reference contract's paused() view returns the actual pause state (reflecting _pause/_unpause changes), whereas the mutant always returns false; thus the invariant is: after calling pause() the contract reports paused() == true and after unpause() it reports paused() == false — the mutant breaks this because paused() always returns false.

For any caller with the LRT_MANAGER role, calling pause() makes paused() return true (contract reports paused state); the mutant that always returns false violates this because paused() never becomes true after pause() for some manager caller inputs.

For any caller, after calling pause() the reference contract's paused() returns true (reporting it is paused), whereas the mutant that hardcodes paused() to false will make paused() return false after pause(), violating this property for some caller inputs.

For any caller, calling pause() when the caller has LRT_MANAGER role causes paused() to return true on the reference; the mutant (which always returns false) will sometimes return false after pause(), violating this rule.

For any caller address, if that caller is granted the LRT_MANAGER role and then calls pause(), the reference contract's paused() view will sometimes return true (i.e. paused can be true) depending on role and calls, whereas the mutant that always returns false cannot report paused()==true after pause(), so there exists inputs (a manager caller) where paused() differs — we assert that when a manager pauses, paused() becomes true.

For any state of the contract, the public getter paused() must return the actual _paused boolean (i.e. paused() == _paused); the mutant negates the stored value so paused() returns !_paused and thus violates this rule for some inputs.

For any input address, the reference contract rejects setting lrtConfig to the zero address (updateLRTConfig reverts or otherwise disallows zero), but the mutant allows storing the zero address — so the property is that calling updateLRTConfig(zero) is always disallowed by the reference and allowed by the mutant for some input (the zero address).

The reference contract ALWAYS rejects (reverts) calls to updateLRTConfig when the provided address is the zero address, whereas the mutant allows storing the zero address; thus for some input (address(0)) the mutant accepts the update while the reference rejects it.

For every caller that currently has the LRT admin role, calling updateLRTConfig with any NON-ZERO address succeeds (reference allows only non-zero addresses), while the mutant additionally allows the ZERO address; thus the invariant: after a successful updateLRTConfig from an admin, lrtConfig() getter (public state) is never the zero address — the reference preserves this for all inputs, the mutant can break it when the admin passes address(0).

For every caller (admin) and every nonzero or adversarial address input, after calling updateLRTConfig the stored lrtConfig address is nonzero (reference enforces non-zero), while the mutant can result in lrtConfig becoming zero when given address(0).

For any caller that is an LRT admin and any nonzero address target, calling updateLRTConfig(target) always results in c.lrtConfig() equaling that nonzero target (the reference enforces the target is nonzero), whereas the mutant can make c.lrtConfig() become address(0) for some input (when the admin passes address(0)); thus the invariant: if updateLRTConfig returns (does not revert) then c.lrtConfig() != address(0) holds for all inputs on the reference but is violated by the mutant for some input.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address input, after calling updateLRTConfig(addr) the contract's public lrtConfig getter equals the emitted UpdatedLRTConfig address; the mutant emits the event before storing so the emitted address can differ from the stored lrtConfig for some inputs.

For any nonzero lrtConfigAddr, after calling updateLRTConfig(lrtConfigAddr) the stored lrtConfig() getter equals the address emitted in the UpdatedLRTConfig event; the mutant emits the event before storing so for some addresses the emitted address can differ from the stored lrtConfig(), breaking the property.

After calling updateLRTConfig(addr) with a non-zero address, the reference contract's UpdatedLRTConfig event argument always equals the new lrtConfig() stored value at the time the call returns; the mutant emits the event before storing, so for some addresses the emitted value can differ from the stored lrtConfig(), violating this invariant.

For any nonzero lrtConfig address, after calling updateLRTConfig(addr) the contract's public lrtConfig() getter equals the address returned by getContract(LRTConstants.LRT_ORACLE) on the newly stored lrtConfig (i.e. updater stores the provided address so subsequent calls to lrtConfig getter return that same address); the mutant emits the event before storing lrtConfig so for some inputs the stored lrtConfig differs from the expected stored value and the property can fail.

For any nonzero lrtConfigAddr, after calling updateLRTConfig(lrtConfigAddr) the contract's public lrtConfig() getter equals the argument passed (the reference stores the provided address before/at the observable time), whereas the mutant can emit an event with a different address than the finally stored lrtConfig, so there exists an input where the emitted address differs from the stored lrtConfig causing the property to fail when observing stored lrtConfig().

For any caller address, updateLRTConfig(...) should succeed (return normally) when the caller has the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE in lrtConfig; the mutant inverts the check and will make updateLRTConfig revert for callers that actually ARE admins, so there exist inputs (an admin caller and a non-zero lrtConfig address) that make the mutant fail while the reference succeeds.

For any (caller, lrtConfigAddr) where caller is the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE in the provided lrtConfig, calling updateLRTConfig(lrtConfigAddr) should succeed on the reference but the mutant (which inverts the admin check) will revert for such admin callers, so there exists admin caller inputs that break the mutant.

For any address that is granted DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE in the lrtConfig contract, calling updateLRTConfig(lrtConfigAddr) should succeed on the reference C; the mutant inverts the admin check and will revert for such admin callers, so an admin caller makes the mutant fail.

For any caller address that is granted DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE in the supplied lrtConfig contract, calling updateLRTConfig(address) succeeds (returns normally) on the correct contract; the mutant inverts the admin check and causes such admin callers to have updateLRTConfig revert, so there exist admin caller inputs that break the mutant.

For any lrtConfig implementation where a given caller has the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, calling updateLRTConfig(...) by that caller succeeds on the correct contract; the mutant inverts the admin check and causes such admin callers to be rejected (revert), so there exist inputs (an admin caller and a nonzero lrtConfig address) that make the mutant fail.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 (i.e. c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() == 10); the mutant sets it to 20 for some inputs and thus violates this invariant.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference contract always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 (c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() == 10); the mutant sets it to 20 for some valid lrtConfig addresses, violating this invariant.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference contract always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10; the mutant sets it to a different value (20) for some inputs, so there exists an lrtConfig address for which c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() != 10 after initialize.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address, calling initialize(...) on a fresh C instance completes successfully and sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to a constant value 10 in the reference; the mutant sets a different constant (20) for some lrtConfig addresses, so there exist inputs where initialize succeeds but c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() != 10, violating the universal rule that initialize always results in maxNodeDelegatorCount == 10.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address, after initialize(...) returns successfully on a fresh C, the stored maxNodeDelegatorCount equals 10 (the reference sets it to 10; the mutant sometimes sets it to 20 and thus breaks this invariant).

For any non-zero lrtConfigAddr input, after initialize(...) completes the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 (non-zero), whereas the mutant sets it to 0, so the invariant 'c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() != 0' holds for all admissible inputs on the reference but is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

For any non-zero lrtConfigAddr passed to initialize, the correct contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to a non-zero default (10), so c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() != 0 always holds after initialize; the mutant sets it to 0 breaking this invariant for some input addresses.

After calling initialize with any non-zero lrtConfig address, the correct contract always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to at least 1 (non-zero), while the mutant sets it to 0 for those same inputs, so the property is that c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() > 0 after initialize; the mutant violates this for some inputs.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the correct contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to a non-zero value after initialization, while the mutant sets it to zero for some such inputs; the test calls initialize with a fuzzed lrtConfigAddr and asserts c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() != 0 after initialize.

For any non-zero lrtConfigAddr passed to initialize, the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to a non-zero value (10) after initialization; the mutant sets it to 0 for the same input, so the property is that after initialize(lrtConfigAddr) completes, c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() != 0.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address, after initialize(...) completes the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10, but the mutant leaves it at 0 (so the getter maxNodeDelegatorCount() equals 10 in the reference for all inputs while the mutant can produce 0).

After initialize(lrtConfigAddr) completes with any non-zero lrtConfigAddr, the reference C always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount() == 10, whereas the mutant leaves it at 0 for some inputs (non-zero lrtConfigAddr), so the property is that maxNodeDelegatorCount() == 10 for every admissible lrtConfigAddr.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the correct contract always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount() to 10 after initialize returns; the mutant omits that assignment and leaves it 0 for some inputs, so the property is that maxNodeDelegatorCount() == 10 for all non-zero lrtConfigAddr.

For every non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize(...), the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount() to a non-zero value (10) after initialize returns; the mutant leaves it at zero for some inputs, so the property checks that maxNodeDelegatorCount() != 0 after initialize succeeds.
